articles.title: Unified framework shows thermoelectric performance depends on more than the material itself
articles.description: Thermoelectric materials can directly convert heat into electricity, making them promising for recovering waste heat from factories, vehicles and other sources. They can also transport heat when an electric current is applied through a phenomenon known as the Peltier effect. These properties have attracted considerable interest in energy-saving technologies and thermal management.

articles.title: Southern Ocean may flip from carbon sink to carbon source under mitigation scenarios
articles.description: Plans to limit the global temperature rise to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels depend on reaching net-zero emissions and, in many cases, actively removing carbon dioxide (CO2) from the air. While this helps limit extreme weather, sea level rise, ecosystem loss and the risk of triggering irreversible climate tipping points, a new study, published in Science Advances, finds that reducing CO2 levels may have an unexpected effect. Climate simulations used in the study suggest that the Southern Ocean around Antarctica may switch from being an important carbon sink to being a prolific source of carbon.

articles.title: Tiny cyanobacteria may be the secret heroes of ocean carbon sequestration
articles.description: A process known as the biological carbon pump (BCP) moves organic carbon from near the ocean's surface to the ocean floor. That carbon often stays there for hundreds or thousands of years, making the BCP a primary source of carbon sequestration in the oceans. Scientists have thought that relatively large phytoplankton are more efficient at exporting carbon to the deep ocean than tiny cyanobacteria, but new research by Jingjing Zhang and colleagues published in AGU Advances now calls that belief into question.

articles.title: Why are the stars around our galaxy's black hole missing their companions?
articles.description: A new study suggests that the young stars orbiting the Milky Way's central black hole may have a surprisingly ordinary origin. But the black hole's influence may be what makes their origin look more exotic than it really is. Along with shaping their orbits, it may also destroy their stellar companions. The paper outlining this work was published in Astronomy & Astrophysics on Aug. 11.

articles.title: Earth From Orbit Is Unpredictable and Messy. Could 'Liquid' AI Clear the View?
articles.description: Monitoring Earth from above is a messy, inconsistent business. Clouds can block a satellite view, the angle of the Sun can create huge shadows, and orbital paths might not take a system across the same general area for weeks. That inconsistency is hard to deal with for traditional software, and can even confuse standard deep learning algorithms. But, according to a new review paper by researchers Raul-Alexandru Gorgan and Dorian Gorgan of the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, there’s a new type of frontier AI that could be able to help - bio-inspired Liquid Neural Networks.

articles.title: A New Design For A Plasma Engine Fuels On Only Thin Air
articles.description: Choosing what orbit to put a satellite in always comes with trade-offs. When it comes to Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO), between 100-450 km, there are distinct advantages. Remote sensing cameras can take better pictures, comms and radar require less power, and atmospheric drag will automatically clean up dead satellites. But there’s also a cost - air friction requires any satellite in this orbit to use an engine near constantly to stay in orbit, which in turn requires fuel - typically in the form of expensive gases like Xenon. So, as part of his PhD thesis at the University of Stuttgart, which is available in arXiv, Francesco Romano decided to solve that problem by using the very air molecules that cause that friction as fuel for a plasma engine to keep satellites aloft indefinitely in VLEO.

articles.title: To watch and watch for: Week of Sept. 13
articles.description: The Arts & Entertainment editors welcome everybody old and new to campus for the 2026-2027 academic year! Before classes start to truly ramp up with endless assignments and back-to-back exams, we'd like to offer some suggestions to occupy the free time you may get during this early semester period. Or maybe, you're already piled up with new academic responsibilities and require a much needed break; whatever the case, we've got you covered. If you're looking to feel less stressed about your own life, you can find some comfort in knowing that there's a Resident Evil protagonist out there going through a relentless, inescapable nightmare. Zack Cregger, best known for his critically acclaimed horror films like Barbarian (2022) and Weapons (2025), debuts his Resident Evil (2026) movie this week. Instead of attempting to adapt an interactive, longform video game, which many of the other Resident Evil movies have done, Cregger opted to write a script that parallels the events of Resident Evil 2 in a more modern era rather than a strict recreation of the game. This new, exciting take on the franchise seems promising; and considering Cregger's past filmography, Resident Evil (2026) should be a monumental treat for any fan of horror. Perhaps you're looking for a less explicitly terrifying experience - if you are, Exit Party might be the perfect read. Emily St. John Mandel is best known for her award-winning novel Station Eleven , an examination of what happens when society collapses after a flu pandemic, and Exit Party explores similar ideas of societal decay. It's set in 2031, and America is at war with itself, but the Republic of California has been declared and residents of L.A. are going to a party to celebrate. However, this party seems to fracture reality in more ways than one. Exit Party explores shadowed worlds and fractured timelines as its characters search for answers. Ruminating on life is an integral part of any lived experience, and beabadoobee's music offers an upbeat, catchy way to do so. The alt-rock singer-songwriter releases her fourth studio album, Pylon , this Friday. "Sun Has Set," the album's lead single, features her familiar indie rock-pop beats and introspective lyrics about a closing relationship. Pylon also features collaborations with Hayley Williams and Brendan Yates , so we can expect that the rest of the album is worth a listen. There's not much more you can do to relax than listen to poetry, and The Writing Seminars Reading Series will host a poetry lecture from Matthew Zapruder on Sept. 16 . During the 2016-2017 year, Matthew Zapruder held the annually rotating position of editor for the Poetry Column for The New York Times Magazine , and he is currently the editor at large at Wave Books . He is the author of six collections of poetry, with his most recent I Love Hearing Your Dreams out from Scribner. Don't miss this lecture from a great contemporary poet! To watch: Resident Evil , directed by Zach Cregger - Sept. 18 The Weight , directed by Padraic McKinley - Sept. 18 Bad Apples , directed by Jonatan Etzler - Sept. 18 Tiny Fugitives , directed by Michael Lewen - Sept. 18 Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom , directed by Steve Cox and Matthew Walker - Sept. 18 To read: Exit Party , written by Emily St. John Mandel - Sept. 15 Hollow Bones , written by Jodi Picoult - Sept. 15 American Nightmare , written by Kelly McWilliams - Sept. 15 Deadly Little Lessons , written by Danielle Valentine - Sept. 15 After Year Zero: On Postwar German Thought , written by Fredric Jameson - Sept. 15 To listen: Pylon , by beabadoobee - Sept.18 Day and Night , by Carly Rae Jepsen - Sept. 18 Bass Persuades , by Miley Cyrus - Sept. 18 Mule , by Orville Peck - Sept. 18 Nocturne , by Wasia Project - Sept. 18 Live events: The Writing Seminars Reading Series: Matthew Zapruder Turnbull Lecture - Sept. 16, 6-7 p.m. at Gilman 50 This event is free. articles.title: Male Fruit Fly Brain Trained to Play Doom
articles.description: Last week, Google announced that it managed to produce a detailed 3D reconstruction of an adult male fruit fly's brain and central nervous system. A few days later a software engineer at Coinbase said the fly brain was being trained to play the original Doom. "Each Doom frame stimulates sensory neurons," says Alex Wormuth. "Neural activity is mapped to game controls. Damage triggers a stimulus to two PPL101 dopamine cells as reinforcement." Since then, the digital brain model has been repurposed to control other games like Beat Saber and Super Mario 64. PC Gamer reports: You can even watch the fruit fly play in real time via Wormuth's website, and it not only shows the point of view in Doom, but can also show a third-person render of the fly going around Doom maps. As of the time of writing, the fly is on round 6385 and, well, it's not very good. Sorry, fly. But modders aren't done here. They have also somehow managed to make the fruit fly play Beat Saber, and play it pretty well. Lyra Bubbles on X has used the brain and replays of a song in Beat Saber to teach the fruit fly where to hit and why, via Reinforcement Learning. That does mean it's not organically reacting to the notes popping up on screen, but it is receiving input and responding to stimuli. Lyra says, "Further training is to reduce reliance on external signals and allow it to play fully reactively with no input data." And, after "pivoting to fly engineering in 2026", Jessica Paquette also shared on X their experience running the digital fly brain through Super Mario 64. If you think that is all the game's modders made the fruit fly play, think again, as YouTuber Ro0oney even put it in Minecraft. But this time, Ro0oney used Flywire.AI, a similar project made in collaboration with Princeton University. The number of neurons are different (160,000+ vs 139,255), and Google analyzed a male brain whilst Flywire analyzed a female brain, but the basic idea is the same. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Bridging interfacial water structure and reactivity in photocatalytic hydrogen evolution at TiO2 interfaces
articles.description: Hydrogen (H2) evolution via photocatalytic water splitting is an environmentally friendly and sustainable technology for solar-to-chemical energy conversion. Although interfacial interactions are recognized as key determinants of photocatalytic performance, systematic experimental studies explicitly targeting the structure and reactivity of the water-catalyst interface remain limited. A major challenge lies in probing the molecular structure of interfacial water, especially under hydrogen-evolving conditions.

articles.title: How one RNA nucleotide switch activates fluorescent dyes
articles.description: RhoBAST is a tiny RNA molecule that activates fluorescent dyes, enabling researchers to track RNA molecules in living cells with super-resolution. An international collaboration, which includes Ronald Micura and his team from the Institute of Organic Chemistry, has now shown that a small, local "nucleotide flip" within the RNA controls this fluorescence activation.

articles.title: Bite, buzz, release: How bees make flowers give up their pollen
articles.description: Life is not always easy for a bee: Not all plants place their pollen outside. Some flowers have to be set to vibrating before the pollen can get out of their tube-like stamens. Certain bee species have developed a special technique for this: They bite on the flower and use their flight muscles to generate rapid vibrations. The stamen is shaken and the pollen is released. This phenomenon is known as "buzz pollination."

articles.title: Smart pen detects pressure and movement to identify children's writing difficulties sooner
articles.description: A study by Politecnico di Milano and the University of Insubria (Varese and Como) has been published in PLOS Digital Health. The study involved more than 700 children from primary and lower secondary school. The participants used the THInkPen (Tele-Health Ink Pen) while completing two BVSCO-3 tasks from the Battery for the Clinical Assessment of Writing and Orthographic Skills. This is the most widely used test in Italy for assessing writing difficulties, dysgraphia and dysorthography.
